items.title: Bartlett made the first noble gas compound in 1962
items.claim: Until 1962 every chemistry textbook said noble gases were entirely unreactive. Neil Bartlett at UBC noticed that O2's ionisation energy (1175 kJ/mol) almost matches xenon's (1170). PtF6 had stripped an electron from O2. So PtF6 should be able to oxidise xenon. He tried it. XePtF6 formed instantly.
items.prompt: Why did this single result change inorganic chemistry?

options.text: It broke the assumed inviolability of the noble-gas 'rule of full octets' and opened the chemistry of an entire group of elements that had been written off as inert

items.reveal:
Bartlett's noticed PtF6 (a deep red solid) turned air red on contact: PtF6 had oxidised O2 to O2+ PtF6-. He looked up xenon's ionisation energy, saw the near-equality with O2, and reasoned that PtF6 should also oxidise xenon.

The synthesis (Vancouver, March 1962) used a gas-handling apparatus he had built himself. Within months, Claassen, Selig and Malm at Argonne produced XeF4 by simply heating xenon with fluorine at 400°C.

Today: XeF2, XeF4, XeF6, XeO3, XeO4, KrF2, ArF (the last only at cryogenic temperatures). Bartlett died in 2008. His insight made the chemistry of noble gases a real subject overnight.
items.why: Chemistry has 'laws' that turn out to be untested generalisations. A single decisive experiment can break a 70-year consensus.

items.title: A buffer works best when pH = pKa — even though that means it's only half-effective
items.claim: A buffer is maximally effective at resisting pH change when [HA] = [A-], which means pH = pKa by Henderson-Hasselbalch. Counter-intuitively, this is when only half the acid is dissociated — not when you've added the most base.
items.prompt: Why does maximum buffering happen at half-neutralisation?

options.text: Because half-neutralisation is the only stable condition
Adding acid converts A- to HA and vice versa; the ratio [HA]/[A-] changes most slowly when the two are equal — small additions barely shift the log of the ratio, so pH barely changes
Buffers cannot work outside pH = pKa
Acid and base cancel only at pKa

items.reveal:
Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]).

If [HA] = [A-] (i.e. pH = pKa), then log term = 0 and small changes in [A-] or [HA] barely shift pH. Capacity is maximised within ±1 pH unit of pKa.

Move far from pKa and a buffer collapses: at pH = pKa + 2, [A-]/[HA] = 100; adding more acid takes it from 100 to 50 — only a 0.3 pH change at first, but the conjugate base is rapidly used up.

This is why biological buffers are tuned to the physiological pH they need to defend: phosphate (pKa2 = 7.2) inside cells, carbonate-bicarbonate (open system at pH 7.4) in blood. Choosing pKa to match the target pH is buffer design 101.
items.why: Maximum effectiveness coincides with 'only half the acid is reacted' — a useful surprise that follows directly from the log.

items.title: Some oxides react with BOTH acids and alkalis
items.claim: Sodium oxide reacts with acids only (it's basic). Sulfur trioxide reacts with alkalis only (acidic). But aluminium oxide and zinc oxide react with both — they are amphoteric.
items.prompt: What makes an oxide behave as both acid and base?

options.text: The element is metallic enough to lose electrons AND non-metallic enough to gain them
They are unstable and decompose in either

items.reveal:
Al2O3 + 6 HCl → 2 AlCl3 + 3 H2O (acts as base, accepting protons).
Al2O3 + 2 NaOH + 3 H2O → 2 Na[Al(OH)4] (acts as acid, accepting OH-).

Elements whose oxides are amphoteric sit near the diagonal that separates metals from non-metals on the periodic table — Be, Al, Ga, Ge, Sn, Pb, Sb. Their bonds with oxygen are intermediate in character: not fully ionic (like Na-O), not fully covalent (like S-O).

The Bayer process for extracting aluminium from bauxite uses amphoteric chemistry directly: hot NaOH dissolves Al2O3 from a mixture with iron oxide and silica; iron oxide doesn't dissolve and is filtered off.
items.why: Acid-base behaviour is taught as a binary classification. The boundary is fuzzy — and the fuzzy region is industrially crucial.
